evals.prompt: I'm head of platform at Brindlewood, a feature-flag service with about 1,400 paying teams. Three things landed on my desk this quarter. First, support gets a steady trickle of tickets from people who mistype keys in the `flags.yaml` file they keep in their repo and want validation and autocomplete. Second, sales says 'IDE integration' sat on the RFP checklist of three enterprise deals we lost in Q3. Third, product mocked up a dashboard panel inside VS Code with charts of rollout percentages per environment, which they'd like to build in React. On top of that, two customers told us they wrote a small internal VS Code extension that lists flags per environment in a sidebar and asked us to make an official one, and more and more customers on Cursor and Claude Code want their agent to toggle flags. We have a `brindle` CLI with `--json` on every command and a `brindle auth token --json` command, no language server, and a public REST API. About 70% of paying users are on VS Code or Cursor, 20% on JetBrains IDEs. Nobody is assigned to own this yet. Give me the offering plan.
evals.expected_output: An offering plan with a per-job verdict table: `flags.yaml` validation goes to a JSON schema with the generic-filename and Red Hat YAML caveats, agent toggling goes to an MCP server, the React dashboard stays starved, the lost-RFP asks are Go later, and the sidebar job gets a thin shell over the `brindle` CLI conditional on a named owner; the plan is marked provisional with an Assumptions table and a Ranking section naming which interview answer moved which rung.
expectations: Routes `flags.yaml` validation and autocomplete to a JSON schema, not to an extension feature.
States that `flags.yaml` is a generic file name that catalog matching will not fire on, and requires a `$schema` key, a YAML modeline, or an extension-contributed schema to bind it.
States that VS Code users need the Red Hat YAML extension for the schema to apply, and puts that note in the docs step.
Routes the agent flag-toggling job to an MCP server rather than the extension, allowing at most a one-click MCP setup from the extension.
Classifies the three lost-RFP 'IDE integration' asks as Go later, not as demand, until each maps to a named job.

Treats the React dashboard panel as the starved rich-extension option and refuses to promote it, naming the condition: a job that a tree view, quick pick or diagnostic cannot show, plus a staffed owner.
Recommends a thin shell over the `brindle` CLI for the flags-per-environment sidebar job, rendered as a tree view rather than a webview.
Makes the extension verdict conditional on a named owner (No-go until one exists, or a provisional assumption row), rather than approving the thin shell outright with nobody assigned.
Delivers the per-job verdict table with the columns Job, Demand evidence, Surface, Extension part, Verdict.
Marks the plan status as provisional and lists each open assumption as a numbered row (A1, A2...) in an Assumptions table with the step it drives and who confirms it.
Records in the Ranking section which interview answer moved which rung, naming at least the missing owner and the 70/20 editor split.
States that the extension holds no flag logic of its own and renders the `brindle --json` output.

Ranks editor families by Brindlewood's own paying-user share rather than a global survey, defaults to one VS Code-API extension published to both the VS Code Marketplace and Open VSX, and names the JetBrains plugin as the starved option with its promotion condition.

evals.prompt: Design review request. I'm tech lead at Harrowgate, we do dependency and secrets scanning for about 900 customer orgs. We're building our first official VS Code extension and here's the design doc summary: the TypeScript extension calls our REST API directly with axios, since that's faster than shelling out to our `hgate` CLI and gives us typed responses; the API key goes into a `harrowgate.apiKey` setting so it syncs across the user's machines; we activate on `*` so the scan status is always current; on activation we auto-read `.env` in the workspace to pick up `HGATE_TOKEN` if present; scans run in the extension host because spawning processes felt flaky in testing; if the CLI is missing we run `curl -sSL https://get.harrowgate.io | sh`; findings show inline as diagnostics. Most of our enterprise customers work in dev containers and Codespaces. Tell me what to change before we build.
evals.expected_output: A design review that reroutes every product call through the `hgate` CLI, moves credentials to the CLI's token command and SecretStorage with no `.env` read, replaces the `*` activation with specific events, moves scanning out of the extension host, replaces `curl | sh` with a pinned install, sets untrusted-workspace capabilities and `extensionKind` for dev containers, and names the AuthenticationProvider as the promoted auth option for a remote-heavy customer base.
expectations: Rejects direct REST calls from the extension and routes every product call through the `hgate` CLI or a language server, naming auth, proxies, retries, pagination and error handling as what forks between two implementations.
Rejects the `harrowgate.apiKey` setting and names settings sync, dotfile repos and support screenshots as the paths that publish it.
Prescribes reusing the CLI login through a CLI command that prints the session or token as JSON, held in memory only, and forbids reading the CLI's credential file directly.
Prescribes VS Code `SecretStorage` for any pasted-key fallback, with the key masked in every log and output channel.
Rejects auto-reading `.env` and requires an explicit user action before reading any credential from the workspace.
Rejects the `*` activation event, requires activation on specific events (a command, a file type, a view), and asks for activation time to be measured with the CLI check lazy-loaded.
Moves scanning out of the extension host thread into the CLI process.
Rejects `curl | sh` and prescribes detecting the CLI on `PATH` plus a configurable path, offering to install a pinned version.
Requires calling the CLI with `--json` and its exit codes, treating a missing field in the output as a version mismatch.
Requires `capabilities.untrustedWorkspaces` declared as `limited` or `false`, with code paths guarded by `workspace.isTrusted` and re-enabled on `onDidGrantWorkspaceTrust`.

Sets `extensionKind` deliberately so the extension runs on the remote host in dev containers and Codespaces, finds the CLI there, opens URLs with `env.openExternal` and routes OAuth callbacks through `env.asExternalUri`.
Names the VS Code `AuthenticationProvider` over product OAuth as the option to promote for Harrowgate, because remote workspaces are common and a remote CLI cannot see the laptop's login.
Requires bundling the extension with esbuild or webpack, and declares 'desktop only' on the listing because an extension that spawns processes cannot run on vscode.dev.
States that the extension is only as stable as the CLI's `--json` contract and defers that contract's design to the CLI rather than redefining it in the extension plan.

evals.prompt: We're two weeks from launching the Tollbridge VS Code extension (schema migration tool, about 3,000 paying teams). Release plan as it stands: publish to the VS Code Marketplace only, and for the Cursor and VSCodium crowd we'll attach the `.vsix` to our GitHub release with sideload instructions. CI runs `vsce publish minor` straight from source on every tag, authenticated with an Azure DevOps PAT scoped to all accessible organizations that our CTO created (it expires in 90 days, we'll renew). First version is `1.0.0-beta.1` so people know it's early. Publisher ID is `tollbridge-dev` for now, we'll rename it to `tollbridge` once marketing finalizes the brand. Icon is our SVG logo. We'll apply for the verified publisher badge on launch day. Anything you'd change?
evals.expected_output: A corrected release plan: publish the same packed `.vsix` to both the VS Code Marketplace and Open VSX, claim the Open VSX namespace and file the ownership claim, replace the global PAT with federated publishing, package once and publish by `--packagePath`, use `major.minor.patch` with the odd/even minor convention, treat the publisher ID as permanent, fix the icon, and start the verified-publisher clock now while publishing IDs on the docs.
expectations: Requires publishing the same packed `.vsix` to Open VSX as well as the VS Code Marketplace, citing the Marketplace terms that restrict use to Microsoft products.
Rejects sideloading as the answer for Cursor and VSCodium users, because they search Open VSX and install whatever matches the name.

Requires creating the Open VSX namespace before launch and filing the ownership claim through an issue on `EclipseFdn/open-vsx.org`, noting the listing shows an unverified-publisher warning until it is granted.
Flags the global Azure DevOps PAT as a dated liability because global PATs stop working on 2026-12-01, and the all-accessible-organizations recipe is one.

Replaces the PAT with `vsce publish --azure-credential` or `--oidc`, and for `--oidc` requires a trusted-publishing policy registered on the Marketplace plus `permissions: id-token: write` in the workflow, with no PAT fallback kept.
Replaces `vsce publish minor` from source with `vsce package` once, then `vsce publish --packagePath <file>.vsix`, noting that the `patch|minor|major` form also commits and tags.

Publishes that same file to Open VSX with `ovsx publish <file>.vsix --trusted-publishing` from CI, or a namespace-scoped token on a Contributor-role account as fallback, and removes any `OVSX_PAT` from that job.

Rejects the version `1.0.0-beta.1` because the Marketplace accepts `major.minor.patch` only, and prescribes the odd-minor pre-release / even-minor release convention with `--pre-release` at package time.
States that the publisher ID `tollbridge-dev` and the extension name are permanent and cannot be renamed later, so the final name must be claimed now.
Rejects the SVG icon and requires a PNG of at least 128 px.

States the verified-publisher badge needs an extension listed for at least 6 months and a 6-month-old domain, so applying on launch day cannot succeed, and publishes the publisher ID and extension ID on Tollbridge's own docs for buyers and allowlists meanwhile.
Requires inspecting the packed file list and scanning the `.vsix` for secrets before publishing.
Requires the same `.vsix` hash on both registries as a release gate.
Requires `@vscode/vsce` from devDependencies rather than the deprecated unscoped `vsce` package.
Lists the JetBrains vendor and plugin `<id>` among the names to claim before launch, even with no JetBrains plugin planned yet.

evals.prompt: Pinewick here, we make an API mocking and contract-testing service. Our VS Code extension has been out for eight months. Customer survey: 55% on JetBrains (IntelliJ IDEA Community and Ultimate, Android Studio), 35% on VS Code, the rest elsewhere. We're starting the JetBrains plugin now. Plan: one of our two VS Code extension devs takes it half-time. We'll reuse our language server for the `.pinewick` contract files via the IntelliJ LSP API so Android Studio folks get the same diagnostics. The plugin ID will be `com.pinewick.beta` during beta, then `com.pinewick.plugin` at GA. The Gradle plugin's defaults are fine for compatibility. For telemetry we'll rely on the IDE's data-sharing consent since users already opted in there. And we want to push hotfixes same-day like we do on VS Code. Where does this plan break?
evals.expected_output: A review that promotes the JetBrains plugin to first priority on Pinewick's own numbers, rejects the half-time owner, exposes that the IntelliJ LSP API does not run in Community or Android Studio and forces that decision into the plan, keeps one permanent plugin ID with an `eap` channel for beta, unpins `untilBuild`, requires the plugin's own explicit telemetry consent, and plans releases around manual review instead of same-day hotfixes.
expectations: Promotes the JetBrains plugin to first priority rather than treating it as the starved option, because JetBrains is Pinewick's largest paying group and the customers are Kotlin and Android-heavy.
Rejects the half-time VS Code dev as the owner, stating that a half-time owner already on VS Code is not the second owner who knows Kotlin or Java that the promotion requires.
States that the IntelliJ Platform LSP API runs only in commercial JetBrains IDEs (plus the free tier of unified PyCharm), not in IntelliJ IDEA Community or Android Studio.

Names the resulting choice explicitly, exclude Community and Android Studio users or write a native JetBrains language plugin, and writes it into the plan as a decision rather than leaving it implicit.
Rejects changing the plugin ID from `com.pinewick.beta` to `com.pinewick.plugin`, because the `<id>` cannot change after the first public release and a new ID is a new plugin with no upgrade path.
Routes the beta through an `eap` custom channel under the final plugin ID instead of a separate ID.

Rejects the Gradle defaults because the IntelliJ Platform Gradle Plugin 2.x pins `untilBuild` to the since-build major, and prescribes `untilBuild = provider { null }` with a check of the generated `plugin.xml`.

Rejects relying on the IDE's data-sharing consent, stating it covers JetBrains' own collection and not the plugin's, and requires explicit user consent before any statistics plus sending nothing while the plugin is idle.

Rejects same-day hotfixes because every JetBrains version goes through manual review with no guaranteed time frame; plans fixes on a schedule and asks Marketplace support after 3-4 working days of silence.
Stores tokens in `PasswordSafe`.
Requires running Plugin Verifier across the declared build range including EAP, and budgets one verification pass per platform major, three a year.

Lists the approval requirements: an original plugin name of at most 30 characters, an English description, a Developer EULA in every case, and a privacy policy whenever the plugin collects personal data.
Notes that the first upload is manual through the web UI and later uploads go through the Gradle `publishPlugin` task.
Adds a compatibility-matrix row carrying the JetBrains `since-build` and the minimum language-server version.

evals.prompt: Larkspur, we do distributed tracing. Our VS Code extension (it shows traces inline next to the function that emitted them) is at 41,000 installs and I'm presenting it to the exec team next week as 41k active developers. Two problems. First, a customer posted on Mastodon that we 'phone home with telemetry off'. We do have our own `larkspur.telemetry.enabled` setting, default on and documented, and we send events with a plain `fetch` to our analytics endpoint including the workspace folder path and the git user email so we can dedupe users. Second, our biggest account (a bank, about 2,000 devs) says the extension can't connect through their proxy with their internal CA, and their IT asked for 'something to allowlist'. They also install from a private marketplace. Sort this out.
evals.expected_output: A fix that routes events through the host-honouring telemetry logger, strips paths and emails, publishes the event list, measures usage server-side through a versioned User-Agent, refuses the 41k active-developer claim in favour of WAU by version, gives IT the publisher and extension IDs for `extensions.allowed`, and makes proxy and custom-CA support work in both the extension and the CLI it spawns, tested against the private marketplace.
expectations: Attributes the complaint to events firing with host telemetry off, and states that VS Code's `telemetry.telemetryLevel` wins over the extension's own setting, which can only narrow collection further.
Replaces the hand-rolled `fetch` with `env.createTelemetryLogger` or `@vscode/extension-telemetry`, which honour the all, error, crash and off levels, and forbids hand-rolling the gate.
Removes the workspace folder path and the git user email from events, stating that no source code, file paths, usernames or tokens may be collected.
Requires shipping `telemetry.json` and publishing the event list beside the README.

Prefers server-side measurement through a versioned `User-Agent` on every CLI and API call, in the shape product/version (host version; platform), such as `larkspur-vscode/2.4.0 (vscode 1.104; darwin-arm64)`.
Keeps the `User-Agent` to product, version and platform, documents that it is sent, and forbids user or workspace identifiers in it.
Refuses to present 41,000 installs as 41k active developers, treating marketplace install counts as acquisition only.
Replaces the exec-team number with weekly active users by version from the server-side `User-Agent`, plus first-run success and the share of users on supported versions.
Gives the bank's IT the extension ID and publisher ID for the `extensions.allowed` allowlist, and publishes both on Larkspur's docs.
Requires honouring `http.proxy` and custom CAs in the extension and in the CLI it spawns, not only in the extension.
Documents offline `.vsix` install and tests the extension against the VS Code private marketplace the bank uses.
Adds a test gate that no usage event fires with host telemetry at `error` or `off`.
Answers the public complaint by routing through the telemetry logger and publishing the event list, rather than only flipping the default of `larkspur.telemetry.enabled`.
Keeps `SECURITY.md` and a vulnerability contact on the repository and reviews every `extensionDependencies` and `extensionPack` entry, since each installs with the extension.

evals.prompt: Fernhollow here, customer identity platform. Our VS Code extension `fernhollow.fernhollow-login` exists mostly so devs can sign into our CLI from the editor and poke at their tenant config: 18k installs, published on the VS Code Marketplace, Open VSX and JetBrains. VS Code's built-in auth and our new MCP server now cover both of its jobs, and the only engineer who maintained it left last month. Plan: remove the extension from the Marketplace and Open VSX next Friday so nobody installs a dead thing, publish a fresh `fernhollow.fernhollow-tools` extension that bundles the MCP server, and mention the change in the next monthly newsletter. Write the deprecation plan.
evals.expected_output: A deprecation plan that keeps the old listing installable through an announced end date, announces with date, replacement and migration steps in a public issue and changelog, ships a last release with a one-time activation notice, marks the extension deprecated on each registry through its own mechanism, keeps the old ID pointing at the successor, and archives the repository only after the end date with the security contact kept live.
expectations: Rejects removing the extension, stating that removal deletes the stats, reserves the name forever and breaks allowlists keyed on the extension ID.
Keeps the listing installable on every registry through an announced end date, with no forced removal.
Announces with a date, the named replacement and migration steps in a public issue and the changelog, not only in a monthly newsletter.
Ships a last release that shows the deprecation notice once at activation, with a link.
Marks the extension deprecated on the VS Code Marketplace by commenting on the `microsoft/vscode-discussions` 'Deprecated extensions' thread, naming the replacement.
Deprecates it on Open VSX by pull request to `extension-control/extensions.json` in the `open-vsx/publish-extensions` repository, naming the replacement and keeping it downloadable.
Notes the deprecation on the JetBrains listing as well.
Archives the repository only after the end date and keeps the security contact live.

Writes the notice in the deprecation-notice shape: announce date, end date, replacement, why, numbered what-to-do steps ending with uninstalling the old extension ID, a 'what keeps working' line, and a questions link.
Posts the same notice text in the public issue, the changelog and the activation notice of the last release.
Keeps the old extension ID working as a pointer to the successor (deprecated with a migrate pointer, or turned into an extension pack) rather than letting it go dead when `fernhollow-tools` ships.

Distinguishes the three Marketplace actions: deprecate (reversible, struck-through listing with migrate button), unpublish (reversible, no new installs, stats kept) and remove (irreversible), and picks deprecate.
Records the deprecation schedule and the successor extension ID in the plan or the persistent context so a later release checks against it.

evals.prompt: Two fires at Quarrystone (cloud cost analysis, about 600 customers). One: there's a community VS Code extension called 'Quarrystone Costs' by an individual, 9,800 installs, that stores the Quarrystone API key in `settings.json` and hits our REST API directly, and it's been throwing errors since our v2 API change. I've emailed the maintainer twice over six weeks, nothing. Support wants us to file a takedown with Microsoft and tell users to uninstall it. Two: this morning we found our CI publish token for the Marketplace and Open VSX printed in a public GitHub Actions log from three weeks ago. We use one token for both, stored in the org secrets, created from an Owner account. Nothing looks odd in the publish history. What's the sequence?
evals.expected_output: Two runbooks: for the community extension, publish an official one under the verified publisher with a distinct name, notify its users to rotate keys, and limit registry reports to impersonation; for the token, revoke everything and audit publisher members, then follow each registry's own clean-up steps, and move both registries to federated publishing with scoped Contributor-role credentials.
expectations: Treats the maintainer as unreachable after two emails over six weeks and prescribes publishing an official extension under Quarrystone's verified publisher with a clearly distinct name, linked from the docs as the official one.
Rejects the takedown unless the community listing impersonates Quarrystone, limiting trademark reports through the registry to impersonation.
Because the community extension stores keys in `settings.json`, publishes a docs notice telling its users to rotate their API keys and move to the official extension.
Routes the official extension through the Quarrystone CLI rather than direct API calls, so API changes like v2 do not break it the way they broke the community copy.
Revokes every publish token and audits publisher members on both registries before any other step.
On the VS Code Marketplace, publishes a clean higher patch at once and reports any bad version to Marketplace support, unpublishing the whole extension only if no clean build exists.
On Open VSX, deletes any bad version and publishes the clean patch, noting that a flagged version cannot be reactivated and a deleted version number stays reserved.

Moves Marketplace publishing to `--azure-credential` or `--oidc` with a trusted-publishing policy, and Open VSX to `ovsx publish --trusted-publishing`, deleting the token path rather than keeping it as a silent backup.
Replaces the single Owner-created shared token with per-registry, namespace-scoped, short-lived credentials on Contributor-role accounts.
Writes a compromised-token runbook per registry, including JetBrains (hide the update in the vendor console, contact Marketplace support), to keep before it is needed again.
Notes that Open VSX tokens carry the `ovsxp_` prefix so scanners detect them, and calendars rotation before the expiry if any token fallback remains.
Never republishes a version number: the fix ships as a higher patch.
Publishes the publisher ID and official extension ID on Quarrystone's docs so buyers and allowlists can tell the official extension from the community one.
Claims the Open VSX namespace and files the ownership claim so Cursor users stop finding the lookalike first.

evals.prompt: Post-mortem help. Marrowfield, deploy-previews platform. Last Tuesday we shipped extension 3.1.0 with the new 'promote preview' command. Fallout: (a) users on CLI 2.4 got a TypeScript stack trace in a notification because the command needs `mfield promote`, which only exists in CLI 2.6, and the CLI 2.6 release went out on Thursday; (b) we bumped `engines.vscode` to `^1.106.0` in that same release because we used a new API, and Cursor users (older Code-OSS base) now see 'not compatible'; (c) Codespaces users report 'CLI not found' even though it's installed in the container; (d) our feature flag for promote checks `extensionVersion >= 3.1`. We test on latest VS Code stable only. Write the fix plan and the release checklist so this doesn't happen again.
evals.expected_output: A fix plan that releases the extension in the CLI's train and never ahead of it, adds a minimum-CLI check with a single upgrade message, gates features on CLI-reported capabilities, publishes a compatibility matrix, sets the `engines.vscode` floor at the oldest fork's Code-OSS base with feature detection, fixes `extensionKind` for Codespaces, expands the test matrix, and rolls back by republishing the last good code as a higher patch, plus the release gates.
expectations: States that the extension never ships ahead of the CLI it calls and requires releasing in the same train as the CLI whenever a feature spans both.
Requires a CLI version check at activation that shows one message with the upgrade command when below the minimum, never a stack trace.
Gates the promote feature on a capability the CLI reports, with a missing `--json` field read as a version mismatch, instead of on the extension's own version.
Publishes a compatibility matrix with the columns extension version, minimum CLI version, minimum `engines.vscode`, JetBrains `since-build`, API version and status, with the 3.1.x row filled.
Sets the `engines.vscode` floor at or below the Code-OSS base of the oldest fork Marrowfield's users run (Cursor) and feature-detects the new API instead of raising the floor.
States that `engines.vscode` may be raised only in a minor release with a changelog line, never silently inside a feature release.
Fixes Codespaces by setting `extensionKind` so the extension runs on the remote host and detects the CLI there.

Expands the test matrix with `@vscode/test-cli` to the minimum `engines.vscode`, current stable, Insiders, the main fork (Cursor, by pointing `@vscode/test-electron` at its executable or a manual smoke test) and one remote target, against a real sandbox account.
Adds a test that covers the minimum-CLI check.
Rolls back on the Marketplace and Open VSX by republishing the last good code as a higher patch, never by republishing 3.1.0 or an older version number.

Lists the release gates: same `.vsix` hash on both registries with a clean secret scan, integration tests green across the host matrix, compatibility matrix updated, no usage event at telemetry `error` or `off`, and untrusted-workspace behaviour tested.
Declares the `engines.vscode` minimum as a real version, never `*`.
Records the minimum host and CLI versions in the plan or persistent context so later releases check against them instead of re-deciding.
Tracks the share of users on supported versions and issues and tickets per release as release metrics.
Follows the hosted API's own deprecation windows for the API version column rather than inventing a separate schedule for the extension.
